q-134159:
The (population) covariance of the data sets $x={{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}}$ and $y={{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}}$ is given by 

$$
\text{Cov}(x,y)=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),
$$

where $\overset{―}{x}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $\overset{―}{y}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}$ are the means of the data sets.

Therefore, the covariance of our data sets is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(-1-3)(-2-4)+(6-3)(5-4)+(2-3)(7-4)+(5-3)(6-4)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(-4)(-6)+(3)(1)+(-1)(3)+(2)(2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[24+3-3+4] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 28 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

q-149616:
The (population) covariance of the data sets $x={{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}}$ and $y={{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}}$ is given by 

$$
\text{Cov}(x,y)=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),
$$

where $\overset{―}{x}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $\overset{―}{y}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}$ are the means of the data sets.

Therefore, the covariance of our data sets is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(12-7)(-4-(-4))+(7-7)(-6-(-4)) \\  & \,\,\,+(6-7)(-4-(-4))+(3-7)(-2-(-4))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(5)(0)+(0)(-2)+(-1)(0)+(-4)(2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[0+0+0-8] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (-8) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-149561:
The (population) covariance of the data sets $x={{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}}$ and $y={{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}}$ is given by 

$$
\text{Cov}(x,y)=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),
$$

where $\overset{―}{x}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $\overset{―}{y}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}$ are the means of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the means: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (12+12+14+14) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 52 \\  & =13 \\ \overset{―}{y} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (85+90+97+100) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 372 \\  & =93\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance of our data sets is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(12\,-\,13)(85\,-\,93)+(12\,-\,13)(90\,-\,93)+(14\,-\,13)(97\,-\,93)+(14\,-\,13)(100\,-\,93)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(-1)(-8)+(-1)(-3)+(1)(4)+(1)(7)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8+3+4+7] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 22 \\  & =5.5.\end{aligned}
$$

q-134221:
The (population) covariance of the data sets $x={{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}}$ and $y={{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}}$ is given by 

$$
\text{Cov}(x,y)=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),
$$

where $\overset{―}{x}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $\overset{―}{y}=\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}$ are the means of the data sets.

Therefore, the covariance of our data sets is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(7-10)(7-8)+(9-10)(8-8)+(11-10)(9-8)+(13-10)(8-8)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(-3)(-1)+(-1)(0)+(1)(1)+(3)(0)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[3+0+1+0] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-26385:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x-3} & ={7}^{x} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x-3}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({7}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & =\operatorname{log}⁡({7}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(7) & =3 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(7)) & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$

q-66899:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y+1} & ={3}^{2y} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2y})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
y+1=\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2y})\,
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
y+1=2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)
$$

Finally, we solve for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ 2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-y & =1 \\ y(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-1) & =1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

q-242923:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2x} & ={8}^{1-6x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{2x}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({8}^{1-6x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(1-6x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(1-6x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(8))}\end{aligned}
$$

q-100482:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{x+7} & ={5}^{8-4x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x+7}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{8-4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =(8-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =(8-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) \\ x & =\frac{8\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

q-124498:
Using the definition of factorial, we have

$$
(n+3)!=(n+3)\cdot (n+2)\cdot (n+1)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1.
$$

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(n+3)! & =(n+3)\cdot \overset{(n+2)!}{\overset{⏞}{(n+2)\cdot (n+1)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =(n+3)\cdot (n+2)!\end{aligned}
$$

q-124142:
Using the definition of factorial, we have 

$$
(k+2)!=(k+2)\cdot (k+1)\cdot k\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1.
$$

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k+2)! & =(k+2)\cdot \overset{(k+1)!}{\overset{⏞}{(k+1)\cdot k\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =(k+2)\cdot (k+1)!\end{aligned}
$$

q-73023:
First, notice the following:

$$
(n+1)!=(n+1)\cdot n\cdot (n-1)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(n-1)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n+1)!}{(n-1)!} & =\frac{(n+1)\cdot n\cdot (n-1)!}{(n-1)!} \\  & =\frac{(n+1)\cdot n\cdot \cancel{(n-1)!}}{\cancel{(n-1)!}} \\  & =n(n+1)\end{aligned}
$$

q-73028:
First, notice the following:

$$
(n+2)!=(n+2)\cdot (n+1)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(n+1)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+2)!} & =\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+2)\cdot (n+1)!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(n+1)!}}{(n+2)\cdot \cancel{(n+1)!}} \\  & =\frac{1}{n+2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-73037:
First, we notice that

$$
(k+2)!=(k+2)(k+1)!
$$

Then, we can cancel the $k!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(k+2)((k+1)!)^{2}}{((k+2)!)^{2}} & =\frac{(k+2)\cdot (k+1)!\cdot (k+1)!}{(k+2)!\cdot (k+2)!} \\  & =\frac{(k+2)\cdot (k+1)!\cdot (k+1)!}{(k+2)\cdot (k+1)!\cdot (k+2)\cdot (k+1)!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(k+2)}\cdot \cancel{(k+1)!}\cdot \cancel{(k+1)!}}{(k+2)\cdot \cancel{(k+1)!}\cdot \cancel{(k+2)}\cdot \cancel{(k+1)!}} \\  & =\frac{1}{k+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-19882:
First, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}(n+9)! & =(n+9)(n+8)(n+7)! \\ (n-8)! & =(n-8)(n-9)!\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can cancel the $(n+7)!$ and $(n-9)!$ that occur in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n-8)!\,(n+9)!}{(n-9)!\,(n+7)!} & =\frac{[(n-8)\cdot (n-9)!]\cdot [(n+9)\cdot (n+8)\cdot (n+7)!]}{(n-9)!\cdot (n+7)!} \\  & =\frac{(n-8)\cdot \cancel{(n-9)!}\cdot (n+9)\cdot (n+8)\cdot \cancel{(n+7)!}}{\cancel{(n-9)!}\cdot \cancel{(n+7)!}} \\  & =(n-8)\cdot (n+8)\cdot (n+9) \\  & =(n-8)(n+8)(n+9)\end{aligned}
$$

q-70612:
The period of $y=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\operatorname{sec}⁡(x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=3$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\operatorname{sec}⁡(x+2\cdot 3\cdot \pi )=\operatorname{sec}⁡(x+6\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\sqrt{2},$ then $\operatorname{sec}⁡(x+6\pi )=\sqrt{2}.$

q-158049:
First, let's recall the graph of $y=\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13942972/assets/fbf6ef1ca91f998ab4dc2dda1890ffc8a713f2eeff19e5569351b2466256d63a.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ is $2\pi .$

- Our graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis. This means that $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ is an *even* function, and we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(-x)=\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡(-a+20\pi ) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(-a+2\pi \cdot 10) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(-a).\end{aligned}
$$

- Secondly, using the evenness of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡(-a) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡a \\  & =\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sec}⁡(-a+20\pi )=\sqrt{7}.$
